# A block \(\alpha\)-circulant based preconditioned MINRES method for wave equations

Xue-lei Lin<sup>1</sup> and Sean Hon<sup>2</sup>

**Abstract**

In this work, we propose an absolute value block \(\alpha\)-circulant preconditioner for the minimal residual (MINRES) method to solve an all-at-once system arising from the discretization of wave equations. Motivated by the absolute value block circulant preconditioner proposed in [E. McDonald, J. Pestana, and A. Wathen. SIAM J. Sci. Comput., 40(2):A1012-A1033, 2018], we propose an absolute value version of the block \(\alpha\)-circulant preconditioner. Since the original block \(\alpha\)-circulant preconditioner is non-Hermitian in general, it cannot be directly used as a preconditioner for MINRES. Our proposed preconditioner is the first Hermitian positive definite variant of the block \(\alpha\)-circulant preconditioner for the concerned wave equations, which fills the gap between block \(\alpha\)-circulant preconditioning and the field of preconditioned MINRES solver. The matrix-vector multiplication of the preconditioner can be fast implemented via fast Fourier transforms. Theoretically, we show that for a properly chosen \(\alpha\) the MINRES solver with the proposed preconditioner achieves a linear convergence rate independent of the matrix size. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt to generalize the original absolute value block circulant preconditioner in the aspects of both theory and performance the concerned problem. Numerical experiments are given to support the effectiveness of our preconditioner, showing that the expected optimal convergence can be achieved.

_Keywords:_ Block Toeplitz matrix; convergence of MINRES solver; wave equations; absolute value block \(\alpha\)-circulant preconditioners

**Mathematics Subject Classification:** 15B05; 65F08; 65F10; 65M22

### 1. Introduction

Over the past few decades, the development of parallel-in-time (PinT) solvers for evolutionary partial differential equations (PDEs) has been an active research area. Various PinT methods have been proposed and, among these, two types of solvers are particularly of interest<tbc>

<sup>1</sup>School of Science, Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen 518055, China. E-mail: linzuelei@hit.edu.cn <sup>2</sup>The Corresponding Author. Department of Mathematics, Hong Kong Baptist University, Kowloon Tong, Hong Kong SAR. E-mail: seanyshon@hkbu.edu.hk

<tbc>due to their success for a wide range of equations - the parareal method [30] and the multigrid- reduction-in-time [10]. For more on the development of such parallel methods for PDEs, we refer readers to [2-4, 9, 12, 14, 16, 17, 26] and the references therein.

Recently, ever since the inception of the preconditioning method developed in [37], there have been an increasing amount of work on developing effective PinT preconditioners for the all-at-once systems arising from solving evolutionary PDEs (see, e.g., [7, 20, 22, 23, 29]). These methods can be categorized into the so-called all-at-once PDE solvers. In other words, instead of solving the target PDE in a sequential way, they propose a PinT preconditioner for solving the vast all-at-once linear system, which is constructed from stacking all unknowns at each time levels simultaneously. Among these methods, block \(\alpha\)-circulant preconditioners have attracted much attention due to their superior performance for a large class of PDEs, including heat equations [28], wave equations [32, 41], and advection-diffusion equations and viscous Burgers’ equation [44]. However, block \(\alpha\)-circulant preconditioners are nonsymmetric and, therefore, not Hermitian positive definite (HPD). Consequently, they cannot be directly utilized with symmetric preconditioned Krylov subspace solvers such as the minimal residual (MINRES) method. One of the objectives of this work is to bridge this gap, thereby enabling block \(\alpha\)- circulant preconditioners to accelerate the convergence rate of the MINRES solver when solving the all-at-once system.

Letting alone the preconditioner used, the MINRES method is only applicable to solving symmetric linear system. Thanks to the symmetrization technique proposed in [36], the all-at- once system can be equivalently converted into a symmetric linear system by applying a reverse- time ordering permutation transformation. In [37], an absolute value block circulant (ABC) preconditioner was proposed for the symmetrized linear system; this preconditioner is HPD and, therefore, suitable for use with the MINRES solver. The numerical results presented in [37] demonstrate that the MINRES solver, when coupled with the ABC preconditioner, is effective for the symmetrized all-at-once system that arises from parabolic equations. Nevertheless, as will be shown from the numerical examples in Section 3 and the explanations in Remarks 1 & 2, MINRES with the ABC preconditioner does not work well for wave equations. Hence, another objective of this work is to improve the performance of the ABC preconditioner.

Inspired by the ABC preconditioning technique, we consider proposing an absolute-value version of the aforementioned block \(\alpha\)-circulant preconditioner, which is HPD and thus can be used as a preconditioner of MINRES solver. In fact, our proposed absolute value block \(\alpha\)-circulant (ABAC) preconditioner can be seen as an extension of the ABC preconditioner. In other words, when \(\alpha=1\), the ABAC preconditioner reduces to the ABC preconditioner. Like the original block \(\alpha\)-circulant preconditioner, the implementation of the proposed ABAC preconditioner is PinT. Theoretically, we show that the MINRES solver with the proposed ABAC preconditioner has a matrix-size independent convergence rate for solving the symmetrized<tbc>

<tbc>all-at-once linear system from wave equation when \(\alpha\) is properly chosen. Numerical results in Section 3 also show that the ABAC preconditioner outperforms the ABC preconditioner.

More importantly, to the best of our knowledge, our proposed preconditioning method is the first work to show that a nontrivial symmetric positive definite version of block \(\alpha\)-circularant matrix can be constructed for the symmetrized the all-at-once system arising from wave equations, providing a positive answer to the open question discussed in \[32, Section 3\] that the construction and analysis of such a preconditioner is possible. We emphasize that the construction of our proposed preconditioner, involving the use of matrix square root on \(\alpha\)-circularant matrices, has rarely been seen in the relevant literature. Through this novel preconditioning idea, we hope to inspire and stimulate a new line of efficient algorithms for solving other more challenging PDEs, further enriching the PinT solver community.

It is worth noting that the use of ABAC preconditioners has recently been applied to dense block lower triangular Toeplitz systems \[27\]. However, we must emphasize that the theoretical results presented in \[27\] are not applicable to the wave equation considered in this work. This inapplicability arises because \[27, Assumption 1 (ii)\] is not satisfied by the matrix T to be defined in (1.2).

In this work, we are interested in solving the following linear wave equation as a model problem

\(\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
u_{tt}(x,t)=\Delta u(x,t)+f(x,t), & (x,t)\in\Omega\times(0,T], \\
u=0, & (x,t)\in\partial\Omega\times(0,T], \\
u(x,0)=\psi_0,u_t(x,0)=\psi_1, & x\in\Omega.
\end{array}\right.\) (1.1)

For instance, a direct PinT solver was proposed in \[13\] for (1.1), where the so-called diagonalization technique \[33\] was used. For more about the existing solvers based on this diagonalization technique for solving the wave equation, we refer to the recent review paper \[15\].

Unlike a direct solver, we focus on a preconditioned iterative method for the equation in what follows. For solving (1.1), we adopt here the implicit leap-frog finite difference scheme used in \[32, 43\], which was established and shown in \[31\] to be unconditionally stable without the requirement of the restrictive Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) condition on the mesh step sizes. Specifically, given a positive integer _n_, we let \(\tau=\frac{T}{n}\) be the time step size. Let _h_ denote the step size along each spatial direction and let _m_ denote the number of spatial grid points. For _k_=1_,...,n_-1, we have<tbc>

\(\frac{\mathbf{u}_m^{(k+1)}-2\mathbf{u}_m^{(k)}+\mathbf{u}_m^{(k-1)}}{\tau^2}=\Delta_h\frac{\mathbf{u}_m^{(k+1)}+\mathbf{u}_m^{(k-1)}}{2}+\mathbf{f}^{(k)},\)

<tbc>where \(\Delta_h\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) is the second-order discrete matrix approximating the Laplacian operator \(\Delta\) in (1.1), \(\mathbf{u}_m^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times 1}\) is an approximation to \(u(\mathcal{G}_h,k\tau)\), \(\mathbf{f}^{(k)}=f(\mathcal{G}_h,k\tau)\), G_<sub>h</sub>_ denoting the<tbc>

spatial grid points arranged in the lexicographic ordering.

Instead of solving the above equations for \(\mathbf{u}_m^{(k)}\) sequentially for _k_=1,2_,...,n_-1, we consider the following equivalent all-at-once system _mn_-by-_mn_ (real) nonsymmetric block Toeplitz system

\(\underbrace{\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c }
L &  &  &  &  \\
-2I_m & L &  &  &  \\
L & -2I_m & L &  &  \\
 & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots &  \\
 &  &  & L & -2I_m & L
\end{array}\right]}_{=:\mathcal{T}}\underbrace{\left[\begin{array}{ c }
\mathbf{u}_m^{(1)} \\
\mathbf{u}_m^{(2)} \\
\mathbf{u}_m^{(3)} \\
\vdots \\
\mathbf{u}_m^{(n)} \\
\vdots \\
\mathbf{f}_m^{(n-1)}
\end{array}\right]}_{=:\mathbf{u}}=\tau^2\underbrace{\left[\begin{array}{ c }
\mathbf{f}_m^{(0)}/2+\Psi_1/\tau+\Psi_0/\tau^2 \\
\mathbf{f}_m^{(1)}-L\Psi_0/\tau^2 \\
\mathbf{f}_m^{(2)} \\
\vdots \\
\mathbf{f}_m^{(n-1)}
\end{array}\right]}_{=:\mathbf{f}},\) (1.2)

where \(L=I_m-\frac{\tau^2}{2}\Delta_h\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\). Note that _I<sub>m</sub>_ denotes the \(m\times m\) identity matrix.

Throughout, the discrete negative Laplacian matrix \(-\Delta_h\) is assumed HPD and hence _L_ is HPD as well. Such an assumption is easily satisfied when a finite difference method is used on a uniform grid. In a more general case where the spatial domain is irregular and a finite element method is used \[8\], the identity matrix _I<sub>m</sub>_ and \(-\Delta_h\) are replaced by the mass matrix and stiffness matrix, respectively.

We remark that for solving the wave equation (1.1) one can apply other discretization schemes and thus obtain different linear systems other than (1.2). For example, \[7, 20, 23\] concern various time stepping methods while \[41\] adopts the Numerov method.

Thanks to the symmetrization technique proposed in \[36\], we consider to rewrite (1.2) as the following equivalent symmetric form<tbc>

\(\mathcal{YT}\mathbf{u}=\mathcal{Y}\mathbf{f},\) (1.3)

<tbc>where

\(\mathcal{YT}=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c }
 &  & L & -2I_m & L \\
 & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots &  \\
L & -2I_m & L &  &  \\
-2I_m & L &  &  &  \\
L &  &  &  &  \\
\end{array}\right],\) (1.4)

and \(\mathcal{Y}=Y_n\otimes I_m\) with \(Y_n\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) being the anti-identity matrix, i.e., \[_Y<sub>n</sub>_\]_<sub>j,k</sub>_=1 if and only if _j+k=n_+1 and \[_Y<sub>n</sub>_\]_<sub>j,k</sub>_=0 elsewhere. Clearly, the monolithic matrixYT is symmetric since _L_ is assumed symmetric.

For the symmetrized matrix VT given in (1.4), we know from \[11, Theorem 3.4\] and previous<tbc>

results in \[24, 34, 35\] that its eigenvalues can be determined from the so-called generating function of T . According to these results, YT is symmetric indefinite when _n_ is large enough, which accounts for the use of MINRES instead of a HPD Krylov subspace method like the conjugate gradient method in this work. For complete surveys on generating functions as well as other properties of block multilevel Toeplitz matrices, we refer readers to \[5, 6, 18, 19, 38\] and the references therein. Proposed in \[32\], the following block \(\alpha\)-circulant preconditioner can be constructed as an approximation to T : \(\mathcal{C}_\alpha=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c c c c } L & & & & \alpha L & & -2\alpha I_m \\ -2I_m & L & & & & \alpha L & \\ L & & -2I_m & L & & & \\ & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & & & \\ & & & L & & -2I_m & L \end{array}\right].\) (1.5) Clearly, \(\mathcal{C}_\alpha\) is not symmetric and, thus, not HPD. However, Krylov subspace solvers (e.g., MINRES) for symmetric linear systems typically require an HPD preconditioner for maintaining the short-recurrence property. Therefore, \(\mathcal{C}_\alpha\) is not a suitable preconditioner for the symmetric linear system (1.3). To address this issue of positive definiteness, we first note that \(\mathcal{C}_\alpha\) is diagonalizable for \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). To see this, we can rewrite \(\mathcal{C}_\alpha\) as \(\mathcal{C}_\alpha=B_1^{(\alpha)}\otimes L+B_2^{(\alpha)}\otimes(-2I_m),\) (1.6) where \(B_1^{(\alpha)}=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c c c c } 1 & & & \alpha & 0 & & \alpha \\ 0 & 1 & & & \alpha & & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & & & & \\ & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & & & \\ & & & 1 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right],B_2^{(\alpha)}=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c c c c } 0 & & & & & \alpha & \\ 1 & 0 & & & & & \\ 1 & 0 & & & & & \\ & \ddots & \ddots & & & & \\ & & & & & 1 & 0 \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) According to \[1\], \(B_1^{(\alpha)}\) and \(B_2^{(\alpha)}\) are diagonalizable as follows \(B_j^{(\alpha)}=D_\alpha^{-1}\mathbb{F}\Lambda_{\alpha,j}\mathbb{F}^*D_\alpha,j=1,2,\)
\(D_\alpha=\mathrm{diag}(\alpha^\frac{i-1}{n})_{i=1}^n,\mathbb{F}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}[\theta_n^{(i-1)(j-1)}]_{i,j=1}^n,\theta_n=\mathrm{exp}\left(\frac{2\pi\mathbf{i}}{n}\right),\mathbf{i}=\sqrt{-1},\)
\(\Lambda_{\alpha,j}=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{j,k}^{(\alpha)})_{k=1}^n,j=1,2,\lambda_{1,k}^{(\alpha)}=1+\alpha^\frac{2}{n}\theta_n^{2(k-1)},\lambda_{2,k}^{(\alpha)}=-2\alpha^\frac{1}{n}\theta_n^{k-1}.\)

With the diagonalization formulas, \(\mathcal{C}_\alpha\) (\(\alpha\in(0,1)\)) can be shown block diagonalizable as follows<tbc>

\(\mathcal{C}_\alpha=[(D_\alpha^{-1}\mathbb{F})\otimes I_m](\Lambda_{\alpha,1}\otimes L+\Lambda_{\alpha,2}\otimes I_m)[(\mathbb{F}^*D_\alpha)\otimes I_m].\) (1.7)

<tbc>Since _L_ is HPD, \(\Lambda_{\alpha,1}\otimes L+\Lambda_{\alpha,2}\otimes I_m\) is clearly diagonalizable. In other words, \(\mathcal{C}_\alpha\) is similar to a diagonalizable matrix and thus \(\mathcal{C}_\alpha\) itself is diagonalizable for \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). That means for \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) there exists an invertible matrix **X** and a diagonal matrix \(\mathrm{diag}(\mu_i)_{i=1}^{nm}\) such that<tbc>

\(\mathcal{C}_\alpha=\mathbf{X}^{-1}\mathrm{diag}(\mu_i)_{i=1}^{nm}\mathbf{X}.\)

<tbc>Thus, we can define a matrix square root of \(\mathcal{C}_\alpha\) for \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) as follows

\(\mathcal{C}_\alpha^{1/2}=\mathbf{X}^{-1}\mathrm{diag}(\sqrt{\mu_i})_{i=1}^{nm}\mathbf{X},\) (1.8)

where \(\sqrt{\mu_i}\) denotes the principal branch of complex square root of \(\mu_i\).

Consequently, we in this work propose the following HPD preconditioner for YT :

\(\mathcal{P}_\alpha=(\mathcal{C}_\alpha^{1/2})^T\mathcal{C}_\alpha^{1/2}.\) (1.9)

Then, instead of directly solving YT **u**=Y**f**, we employ the MINRES solver to solve the following equivalent preconditioned system

\(\mathcal{P}_\alpha^{-1}\mathcal{YT}\mathbf{u}=\mathcal{P}_\alpha^{-1}\mathcal{Yf}.\) (1.10)

For a real symmetric matrix **H**, denote by |**H**|, the positive semi-definite matrix obtained by replacing eigenvalues of **H** with its absolute value.

**Remark 1.** _When_ \(\alpha=1\), \(\mathcal{P}_\alpha=(\mathcal{C}_1^{1/2})^T\mathcal{C}_1^{1/2}=\sqrt{\mathcal{C}_1^T\mathcal{C}_1}=|\mathcal{C}_1|\) _reduces to the existing ABC preconditioner proposed in \[37\] for heat equations. However, as demonstrated by the numerical results in Section 3,_ P<sub>1</sub> _does not perform well for wave equations. The reason is that the eigenvalues of preconditioned matrix by the ABC preconditioner have outliers away from_ {-1,+1} _and the number of outliers is of_ O(_m), which means the iteration number needed for convergence increases as m increases. This is the motivation for proposing_ \(\mathcal{P}_\alpha\) _in this work. As will be shown, Theorem 13 gives choices of_ \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) _so that the MINRES solver for_ (1.10) _has a linear convergence rate independent of h and_ \(\tau\)_. With guidance of Theorem 13, results in Section 3 show that_ \(\mathcal{P}_\alpha\) _outperforms_ P<sub>1</sub> _for wave equations._

Ultimately, we will show that the preconditioned MINRES solver for the preconditioned system (1.10) achieves a convergence rate independent of \(\tau\) and _h_ and therefore independent of the matrix size.

This paper is organized as follows. We present our main results in Section 2 in which the<tbc>

<tbc>convergence of our proposed preconditioner is analyzed. Numerical tests are given in Section 3 to demonstrate the matrix-size independent convergence rate of the proposed preconditioned MINRES solver.

## 2. Main results

In this section, we discuss properties of our proposed ABAC preconditioner \(\mathcal{P}_\alpha\) defined by (1.9) and the fast implementation for the proposed preconditioned method.

### 2.1. Preliminaries for convergence analysis of the preconditioned method

In this subsection, we introduce preliminaries for the linear convergence rate analysis of MINRES solver for the preconditioned system.

Denote by _GL(K_) the set of all \(K\times K\) invertible complex matrices. For a square matrix **A**, denote by \(\sigma(\mathbf{A})\), the spectrum of **A**. Define

\(\mathcal{Q}(k):=\{\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{C}^{K\times K}|\sigma(\mathbf{A})\subset\mathbb{C}\backslash(-\infty,0]\}.\)

Clearly, \(\mathcal{Q}(K)\subset GL(K)\). For a complex number _z_, denote by \(\Re(z)\) and \(\unknown(z)\), the real part and the imaginary part of _z_, respectively.

**Lemma 1.** _For any_ \(\alpha\in[0,1)\)_, it holds_ \(\mathcal{C}_\alpha\in\mathcal{Q}(mn)\subset GL(mn)\).

**Proof:** See the proof in Appendix **A**.

**Remark 2.** _Clearly, Lemma 1 guarantees that the preconditioner_ \(\mathcal{P}_\alpha\) _is invertible. Moreover, from its proof, we see that the eigenvalues of Strang’s \[40\] block circulant preconditioner_ C<sub>1</sub> _are of form_ \(\mu=2cos(\omega_k)[\lambda cos(\omega_k)-1]+\mathbf{i}2sin(\omega_k)[\lambda cos(\omega_k)-1]\) _and some of which are equal to zero when_ \(\lambda cos(\omega_k)-1=0\)_. Therefore, such an existing block circulant preconditioner may be singular and thus not applicable in general._

Denote by UTT(**v**), the upper triangular Toeplitz matrix with **v** as its first column. Define the _i_-th order Jordan block \(J_i(\lambda)\) as<tbc>

\(J_i(\lambda):=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c c c }
\lambda, & i=1, &  &  \\
\lambda & 1 &  &  \\
 & \lambda & \ddots &  \\
 &  & \lambda & 1 \\
 &  &  & \lambda
\end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{C}^{i\times i},i>1.\)

**Definition 1.** (Matrix function via Jordan canonical form \[21, Definition 1.2\]) _Let_ **A**=**Z**_J_**Z**<sup>-1</sup> _be a Jordan canonical form of a matrix_ \(\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times N}\) _with_<tbc>

\(J=\mathrm{blockdiag}(J_{n_i}(\lambda_i))_{i=1}^k,\{\lambda_i\}_{i=1}^k\in\sigma(\mathbf{A}),\sum_{i=1}^kn_i=N.\)

<tbc>_For a function g of one complex variable that is sufficiently smooth on each point of_ \(\sigma(\mathbf{A})\)_, a matrix function is defined by_<tbc>

\(g(\mathbf{A}):=\mathbf{Z}\mathrm{blockdiag}(g(J_{n_i}(\lambda_i)))_{i=1}^k\mathbf{Z}^{-1},\)

<tbc>_where_ \(g(J_{n_i}(\lambda_i))\) _is an upper triangular Toeplitz matrix given as_

\(g(J_{n_i}(\lambda_i))=\mathrm{UTT}\left(\left(\frac{g(\lambda_i)}{0!},\frac{g'(\lambda_i)}{1!},\dots,\frac{g^{(j)}(\lambda_i)}{j!},\dots,\frac{g^{(n_i-1)}(\lambda_i)}{(n_i-1)!}\right)\right)\in\mathbb{C}^{n_i\times n_i}.\)

For \(z\in\mathbb{C}\), define _s(z_) as the principal branch of complex square root of _z_.

**Proposition 1.** (\[39, Example 1.16\]) _The principal square root function_ \(s(\cdot)\) _is holomorphic on_ \(\mathbb{C}\backslash(-\infty,0]\).

By Definition 1 and Proposition 1, \(s(\cdot)\) as a matrix function is well-defined on Q(_K_) for any positive integer _K_.

Denote \(\mathbb{C}_+:=\{z\in\mathbb{C}|\Re(z)>0\}\).

**Lemma 2.** (\[21, Theorem 1.29\]) _For_ \(\mathbf{A}\in\mathcal{Q}(K)\) _with any positive integer K,_

**(a)** _there exists a unique matrix_ **B** _such that_ **B**<sup>2</sup>=**A** _and_ \(\sigma(\mathbf{B})\subset\mathbb{C}_+\);

**(b)** _the matrix_ **B** _is exactly s_(**A**);

**(c)** _if, additionally,_ **A** _is real, then s_(**A**) _is real._

**Proof:** The results of Lemma 2 come from \[21, Theorem 1.24\] and \[21, Theorem 1.29\]. \(\square\)

Since \(\sigma(\mathcal{T})=\sigma(L)\subset(1,+\infty)\subset\mathbb{C}\backslash(-\infty,0]\), \(\mathcal{T}\in\mathcal{Q}(mn)\). That means _s_(T) is well defined. In the rest of this paper, we use the notation \(\mathcal{T}^\frac{1}{2}\) to represent _s_(T).

**Lemma 3.** _Let_ \(\mathcal{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{mn\times mn}\) _be defined by (1.2). Then,_

**(a)** T<sup>1/2</sup> _is invertible;_

**(b)** T<sup>1/2</sup> _is a real-valued matrix;_

**(c)** YT<sup>1/2</sup> _is symmetric._

**Proof:** As discussed above, \(\sigma(\mathcal{T})\subset(1,+\infty)\). Therefore, \(\sigma(\mathcal{T}^{1/2})\subset(1,+\infty)\), which proves part (a).

Since T is real-valued, Part (b) of Lemma 3 follows from Part (c) of Lemma 2. We now show part (_c_) of Lemma 3. Since VT is symmetric by (1.4) (i.e., VTY-1=T_T_) and (YTY-1)1/2=YT1/2Y-1 by \[21, Theorem 1.13 (c)\], we can see that (YTY-1)1/2=YT1/2Y-1=(T_T_)1/2=(T1/2)_T_, where the last equation follows by \[21, Theorem 1.13 (b)\]. Thus, we readily have shown that YT1/2=(T1/2)_T_Y=(YT1/2)_T_. Part (_c_) is concluded. \(\square\) The following proposition indicates that an ideal preconditioner for VT is the HPD matrix (T1/2)_T_T1/2, which can achieve the optimal two-step convergence when MINRES is used due to the fact that the preconditioned matrix has only two distinct eigenvalues \(\pm 1\). **Proposition 2.** _Let_ \(\mathcal{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{mn\times mn}\) _be defined by (1.2). Then,_ ((T1/2)_T_T1/2)-1YT _has only_ \(\pm 1\) _as eigenvalues._ **Proof:** By Lemma (3) (a), the preconditioner (T1/2)_T_T1/2 is invertible. By Lemma (3) (c), we have YT1/2=(T1/2)_T_Y which yields YT-1/2=(T-1/2)_T_Y. Then, we consider the following preconditioned matrix \(((\mathcal{T}^{1/2})^T\mathcal{T}^{1/2})^{-1}\mathcal{YT}=\mathcal{T}^{-1/2}(\mathcal{T}^{-1/2})^T\mathcal{YT}=\mathcal{T}^{-1/2}\mathcal{YT}^{-1/2}\mathcal{T}\)
\(=\mathcal{T}^{-1/2}\mathcal{YT}^{-1/2}\mathcal{T}^{1/2}\mathcal{T}^{1/2}\)
\(=\mathcal{T}^{-1/2}\mathcal{YT}^{1/2}.\) Thus, we have shown that the preconditioned matrix ((T1/2)_T_T1/2)-1YT is similar to Y which is real-valued, symmetric, and orthogonal. Hence, it has only \(\pm 1\) as eigenvalues. \(\square\) In other words, Proposition 2 provides a guide on designing an effective preconditioner for VT , since in general (T1/2)_T_T1/2 is computationally expensive to implement. In what follows, we shall show that our proposed preconditioner \(\mathcal{P}_\alpha\) approximates the ideal preconditioner (T1/2)_T_T1/2 in the sense that their difference is a small norm matrix whose magnitude is controlled by the parameter \(\alpha\). Its preconditioning effect becomes apparent since \(\mathcal{P}_\alpha\) gets close to (T1/2)_T_T1/2 as \(\alpha\) approaches zero. Now, we turn our focus on the following lemmas and proposition, which will be used to show our main result. For a complex number _z_, denote by \(\Re(z)\) and \(\unknown(z)\), the real part and the imaginary part of _z_, respectively. Similar to Lemma 3, the following lemma on \(\mathcal{C}_\alpha\) is needed. **Lemma 4.** _Let_ \(\mathcal{C}_\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{mn\times mn}\) _be defined by (1.5) with_ \(0<\alpha<1\)_. Then,_ **(a)** \(\mathcal{C}_\alpha^{1/2}\) _is a real-valued matrix;_ **(b)** \(\mathcal{YC}_\alpha^{1/2}\) _is symmetric._

**Proof:** By Lemma 1, \(\mathcal{C}_\alpha\in\mathcal{Q}(mn)\). It is well-known that the image \(s(\mathbb{C}\backslash(-\infty,0])\) is a subset of C<sub>+</sub>. Then, by definition of \(\mathcal{C}_\alpha^{1/2}\) and by the fact that \(\sigma(\mathcal{C}_\alpha)\subset\mathbb{C}\backslash(-\infty,0]\), we have \(\sigma(\mathcal{C}_\alpha^{1/2})\subset\mathbb{C}_+\). Then, Lemma 2 implies that \(s(\mathcal{C}_\alpha)=\mathcal{C}_\alpha^{1/2}\). Moreover, \(\mathcal{C}_\alpha\) is clearly real-valued. Hence, \(\mathcal{C}_\alpha^{1/2}\) is real-valued by part (c) of Lemma 2. Part (a) is shown.

The proof of part (b) of Lemma 4 is similar to the proof of part (c) of Lemma 3. We skip it here.

## 2.2. Convergence analysis of the proposed PMINRES method

In this subsection, we show that the MINRES solver for the preconditioned system (1.10) has a linear convergence rate independent of both \(\tau\) and _h_.

We first provide the following lemma, which will be used to investigate the convergence rate.

For a square matrix **C**, denote by \(\sigma(\mathbf{C})\) the spectrum of **C**. For a real symmetric matrix **H**, denote by \(\lambda_\mathrm{min}(\mathbf{H})\) and \(\lambda_\mathrm{max}(\mathbf{H})\) the minimal and the maximal eigenvalue of **H**, respectively.

**Lemma 5.** _\[8, Theorem 6.13\] Let_ \(\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}\) _and_ \(\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}\) _be a symmetric positive definite matrix and a symmetric nonsingular matrix, respectively. Suppose_ \(\sigma(\mathbf{P}^{-1}\mathbf{A})\in[-a_1,-a_2]\cup[a_3,a_4]\) _with_ \(a_4\ge a_3>0\), \(a_1\ge a_2>0\) _and a_<sub>1</sub>-_a_<sub>2</sub>=_a_<sub>4</sub>-_a_<sub>3</sub>_. ## 2.3. Implementations We begin by discussing the computation of YT **v** for any given vector **v**. Since T is a sparse matrix, computing the matrix-vector product T **v** only requires linear complexity of O(_mn_). As the action of Y is a simple reordering of entries that poses virtually no work, computing YT **v** needs the same complexity. Alternatively, due to the fact that T itself is a block Toeplitz matrix, it is well-known that T **v** (and hence YT **v**) can be computed in O(_mn_log_n_) operations using fast Fourier transforms and the required storage is of O(_mn_). Now, we discuss how to efficiently invert \(\mathcal{P}_\alpha\), based on similar arguments discussed in, for instance, \[28, Section 4\]. The invertibility of \(\mathcal{P}_\alpha\) is guaranteed for \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), which will be proven in the next section. In each iteration of MINRES, it is required to compute \(\mathcal{P}_\alpha^{-1}\mathbf{y}=\mathcal{C}_\alpha^{-1/2}(\mathcal{C}_\alpha^{-1/2})^T\mathbf{y}\) for any given vector **y**. Note that \(\mathcal{C}_\alpha\) is composed of the \(\alpha\)-circulant matrices \(B_j^{(\alpha)}=D_\alpha^{-1}\mathbb{F}^*\Lambda_{\alpha,j}\mathbb{F}D_\alpha\), _j_=1,2, where \(\Lambda_{\alpha,j}=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{j,k}^{(\alpha)})_{k=1}^n\) with \(\lambda_{1,k}^{(\alpha)}=1+\alpha^\frac{2}{n}\theta_n^{2(k-1)}\) and \(\lambda_{2,k}^{(\alpha)}=-2\alpha^\frac{1}{n}\theta_n^{k-1}\). Also, \(D_\alpha=\mathrm{diag}(\alpha^\frac{i-1}{n})_{i=1}^n\) and \(\mathbb{F}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}[\theta_n^{(i-1)(j-1)}]_{i,j=1}^n\) with \(\theta_n=\mathrm{exp}(\frac{2\pi\mathbf{i}}{n})\) and \(\mathbf{i}=\sqrt{-1}\). Considering (1.6) and the eigendecomposition of \(L=U\Lambda U^T\), we have \((\mathcal{C}_\alpha^{-1/2})^T=\big(\big(B_1^{(\alpha)}\otimes L+B_2^{(\alpha)}\otimes(-2I_m)\big)^{-1/2}\big)^T\)
\(=\big(\big(D_\alpha^{-1}\mathbb{F}^*\Lambda_{\alpha,1}\mathbb{F}D_\alpha\otimes U\Lambda U^T+D_\alpha^{-1}\mathbb{F}^*\Lambda_{\alpha,2}\mathbb{F}D_\alpha\otimes(-2I_m)\big)^{-1/2}\big)^T\)
\(=(D_\alpha^{-1}\mathbb{F}^*\otimes U)^{-T}\big(\big(\Lambda_{\alpha,1}\otimes\Lambda+\Lambda_{\alpha,2}\otimes(-2I_m)\big)^{-1/2}\big)^T(\mathbb{F}D_\alpha\otimes U^T)^{-T}.\) Thus, the product \((\mathcal{C}_\alpha^{-1/2})^T\mathbf{y}\) for a given vector **y** can be implemented via the following three steps: \(\text{Step 1: Compute}\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}=(\mathbb{F}D_\alpha\otimes U^T)^{-T}\mathbf{y};\)
\(\text{Step 2: Compute}\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}=\big(\big(\Lambda_{\alpha,1}\otimes\Lambda+\Lambda_{\alpha,2}\otimes(-2I_m)\big)^{-1/2}\big)^T\widetilde{\mathbf{y}};\)
\(\text{Step 3: Compute}\mathbf{z}=(D_\alpha^{-1}\mathbb{F}^*\otimes U)^{-T}\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}.\) When the spatial grid is uniformly partitioned, the orthogonal matrix _U_ becomes a (multi- dimension) discrete sine transform matrix S. In this case, both Steps 1 & 3 can be computed efficiently via fast Fourier transforms and fast sine transforms in O(_mn_log_n_) operations. As for Step 2, the required computations take O(_nm_) operations since the matrix involved is a simple diagonal matrix. In effect, the overall product \(\mathcal{P}_\alpha^{-1}\mathbf{y}=\mathcal{C}_\alpha^{-1/2}(\mathcal{C}_\alpha^{-1/2})^T\mathbf{y}\) can be computed by repeating the above three-step procedure two times. In the case where the underlying differential equation involves variable coefficients, the implementation of our proposed preconditioner can be carried out in a similar way as in the constant-coefficient case. A related discussion will be given in Section 3.

Certainly, when \(\alpha\) is small, computations involving \(D_\alpha^{-1}\) may introduce stability concerns as extensively studied in \[13, 42\]. However, as examined in \[32\], it appears that this does not significantly impact convergence when a Krylov subspace method is used with a properly chosen small \(\alpha\) independent of the meshes. The stability implications of small \(\alpha\) warrant further investigation, which we will address in our future research.

## 4. Conclusions

We have proposed a novel PinT preconditioner \(\mathcal{P}_\alpha\) for the symmetrized all-at-once system of wave equations, YT**u**=Y**f**, whose effectiveness is supported by both theory and numerical evidence. Our preconditioner does not only extend the scope of application of the block \(\alpha\) circulant preconditioning technique to MINRES solver, but also significantly improves the performance of the ABC preconditioner proposed in [37]. As shown in the numerical tests, our proposed preconditioner improves significantly the original ABC preconditioner proposed in [37] in terms of both CPU time and iteration number. The numerical evidence also substantiates the advantages of our proposed strategy, particularly in scenarios where the spatial grid is uniformly partitioned.

## Appendix A Proof of Lemma 1 **Proof:** When \(\alpha=0\), \(\mathcal{C}_\alpha=\mathcal{T}\) . In such case, \(\sigma(\mathcal{C}_\alpha)=\sigma(\mathcal{T})=\sigma(L)\subset(1,+\infty)\subset\mathbb{C}\backslash(-\infty,0]\). Hence, \(\mathcal{C}_0\in\mathcal{Q}(mn)\). It remains to focus on the case \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). We recall from (1.7) that \(\sigma(\mathcal{C}_\alpha)=\sigma(\Lambda_{\alpha,1}\otimes L+\Lambda_{\alpha,2}\otimes I_m).\) Hence, for any \(\mu\in\sigma(\mathcal{C}_\alpha)(\alpha\in(0,1))\), there exists \(k\in\{1,2,\dots,n\}\) and \(\lambda\in\sigma(L)\subset(1,+\infty)\) such that \(\mu=\lambda\lambda_{1,k}^{(\alpha)}+\lambda_{2,k}^{(\alpha)}\)
\(=\lambda-2\alpha^\frac{1}{n}\theta_n^{(k-1)}+\lambda\alpha^\frac{2}{n}\theta_n^{2(k-1)}\)
\(=\lambda-2\alpha^\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{cos}(\omega_k)+\lambda\alpha^\frac{2}{n}\mathrm{cos}(2\omega_k)-2\alpha^\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{i}\mathrm{sin}(\omega_k)+\lambda\alpha^\frac{2}{n}\mathbf{i}\mathrm{sin}(2\omega_k)\)
\(=\lambda-2\alpha^\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{cos}(\omega_k)+\lambda\alpha^\frac{2}{n}(2\mathrm{cos}^2(\omega_k)-1)+\mathbf{i}2\alpha^\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{sin}(\omega_k)[\lambda\alpha^\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{cos}(\omega_k)-1]\)
\(=\lambda(1-\alpha^\frac{2}{n})+2\alpha^\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{cos}(\omega_k)[\lambda\alpha^\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{cos}(\omega_k)-1]+\mathbf{i}2\alpha^\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{sin}(\omega_k)[\lambda\alpha^\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{cos}(\omega_k)-1],\) where \(\omega_k=\frac{2\pi(k-1)}{n}\) . We now show \(\mu\in\mathbb{C}\backslash(-\infty,0]\) case by case. If \(\mathrm{cos}(\omega_k)<0\), then \(\Re(\mu)=\lambda(1-\alpha^\frac{2}{n})+2\alpha^\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{cos}(\omega_k)[\lambda\alpha^\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{cos}(\omega_k)-1]>\lambda(1-\alpha^\frac{2}{n})>0,\) which implies \(\mu\in\mathbb{C}\backslash(-\infty,0]\). If \(\mathrm{cos}(\omega_k)=0\), then \(\Re(\mu)=\lambda(1-\alpha^\frac{2}{n})>0,\) which implies \(\mu\in\mathbb{C}\backslash(-\infty,0]\). If \(\frac{1}{\lambda\alpha^\frac{1}{n}}>\mathrm{cos}(\omega_k)>0\) and \(\mathrm{cos}(\omega_k)\neq 1\), then \(\unknown(\mu)\neq 0\). If \(\mathrm{cos}(\omega_k)=1\), then \(\Re(\mu)=\lambda(1-\alpha^\frac{2}{n})+2\alpha^\frac{1}{n}(\lambda\alpha^\frac{1}{n}-1)=(\alpha^\frac{1}{n}-1)^2+(\lambda-1)(\alpha^\frac{2}{n}+1)>0\). That means \(\mu\in\mathbb{C}\backslash(-\infty,0]\) when \(\frac{1}{\lambda\alpha^\frac{1}{n}}>\mathrm{cos}(\omega_k)>0\). If \(\mathrm{cos}(\omega_k)=\frac{1}{\lambda\alpha^\frac{1}{n}}\), then \(\mu=\lambda(1-\alpha^\frac{2}{n})>0\), which implies \(\mu\in\mathbb{C}\backslash(-\infty,0]\).

If \(\mathrm{cos}(\omega_k)>\frac{1}{\lambda\alpha^\frac{1}{n}}\), then \(\Re(\mu)=\lambda(1-\alpha^\frac{2}{n})+2\alpha^\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{cos}(\omega_k)[\lambda\alpha^\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{cos}(\omega_k)-1]>0\), which implies \(\mu\in\mathbb{C}\backslash(-\infty,0]\).

Hence, if \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), then for any \(\mu\in\sigma(\mathcal{C}_\alpha)\) it holds \(\mu\in\mathbb{C}\backslash(-\infty,0]\). In other words, when \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), it holds that \(\mathcal{C}_\alpha\in\mathcal{Q}(mn)\).

To summarize, for any \(\alpha\in[0,1)\), it holds that \(\mathcal{C}_\alpha\in\mathcal{Q}(mn)\). The proof is complete.
